CRITERIA FOR BASIS OF DRAINAGE POLICY
1. Common Law Rules of Drainage
The common law rules of drainage are found in court decisions declaring principles, practices and customs which have evolved and are commonly accepted without the formality of legislative enactment. The type of common law adopted by the State of Illinois is the civil law rule or what is sometimes referred to as the natural drainage rule.
In its strictest form, the civil law rule recognizes the existence of natural drainage between adjoining lands. The criteria for natural drainage is that one piece of land must be so located that it is at a higher elevation than the adjoining land thereby permitting water to flow naturally from the higher to the lower land.
The owner of the lower land must accept the surface water that naturally drains onto it. On the other hand, the owner of the upper land theoretically can do nothing to change the natural system of drainage to increase the natural flow. Consequently, those acquiring land must expect and are required to accept it, subject to the conditions of nature. There have been many additions, qualifications and restrictions attached to the theoretical concepts of the law and these will be discussed under the various sections of this manual.
The right to drain upon or over the lower owner without making compensation for such a privilege is the same whether the upper land is the property of an individual or is a public highway.
2. Statutory Rules of Drainage
Since the natural drainage rule is generally dependent upon a difference in elevation between adjoining lands, the functioning of this rule ceases when adjoining tracts of land are on equal elevation. Therefore, the legislative branch of the State government has enlarged the common law by the enactment of statutory provisions.
